transcript: In 1919, Boston wasn't destroyed by fire or an earthquake. It was swallowed by a 2 million gallon tsunami of boiling molasses moving at 35 miles per hour. Down on Commercial Street stood a giant 50 -foot steel tank filled with fermenting syrup. It leaked so badly that neighborhood kids collected free syrup in buckets. The company's brilliant solution? They just painted the tank brown so nobody could see the leaks. Then, on an unseasonably warm January afternoon, the rivets popped, like machine gun fire. 2 .3 million gallons of dark, heavy syrup exploded outward in a towering 25 -foot tidal wave. The wave ripped an elevated train track right off its steel girders, smashed entire wooden houses into kindling, and trapped people and horses in waist -deep cooling syrup that hardened like concrete. Firefighters spent weeks pumping millions of gallons of seawater to scrub the city clean, turning Boston Harbor completely brown. And for decades after, locals swear on hot summer days, Boston still smelled like pancakes.
